messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Chukwu's Vigilance

Chukwu was nineteen when the stalking began, though he didn't recognize it as such at first. He had been working as a UX designer at a mid-sized tech firm in Atlanta for just over a year, the kind of role that let him stay quiet in meetings and pour his energy into wireframes and user flows—work that made sense in a way most social interaction didn't. In March, a colleague named Marcus from the marketing department had started messaging him on Slack after hours, asking about his weekend plans, commenting on his Instagram stories within minutes of posting. Chukwu had been polite but distant, a boundary he thought was clear. It wasn't.

By late April, Marcus had begun showing up at the coffee shop where Chukwu went on Tuesday mornings before work. The first time felt like coincidence. The second time, Chukwu felt his stomach tighten. By the fifth time, Marcus was sitting at a table that faced the door, waiting. When Chukwu tried to leave early, Marcus followed him to his car. "I just want to talk," Marcus said, his voice reasonable, almost hurt. "I don't understand why you're being cold." Chukwu drove away, hands shaking on the wheel.

What happened next unfolded in increments that made it hard to know when to panic. Marcus created a fake Instagram account to follow him. He began appearing outside Chukwu's apartment building on random evenings, claiming he "happened to be in the neighborhood." He sent long, rambling messages about how Chukwu had "led him on" and "owed him a chance." When Chukwu blocked him, Marcus found new numbers, new accounts. The messages grew darker—not explicit threats, but close enough: *I know where you live. I know your routine. Don't think you can just ignore me forever.* Chukwu reported it to HR. Marcus was let go. For two weeks, there was silence, and Chukwu had allowed himself to breathe.

Then Marcus appeared at the gym Chukwu had been going to since high school. He was sitting in the lobby when Chukwu came out of the locker room, casual, almost smiling. "Thought I'd try this place," he said. Chukwu left without finishing his workout and never went back.

In the months that followed, Chukwu had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous in ways he couldn't fully control or predict. He had replayed the early interactions with Marcus over and over—the Slack messages, the coffee shop encounters—searching for the moment he had invited this, the way he had acted that had somehow communicated openness or interest. He was certain he had done something, said something, smiled at the wrong moment or been too polite, and that this was the price of that mistake. The thought that he might have inadvertently encouraged Marcus's attention was almost worse than the stalking itself, because it meant the threat came from inside his own judgment.

Now Chukwu had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. He had stopped going to the coffee shop, the gym, the park where he used to sit with his laptop. He varied his route to work, always checking mirrors and blind spots. At the office, he kept his headphones in and his door—when he had one—closed. He had lost weight from the constant low-level anxiety, the way his stomach stayed clenched. His mother had noticed and asked if he was sick. He couldn't explain that he had begun seeing potential threats everywhere: the man at the grocery store who looked at him too long, the car that seemed to slow down on his street, the way his phone buzzed with unknown numbers.

Three months into this vigilance, Chukwu's work had started to suffer. His creative output had flattened; he missed deadlines because he was spending hours checking social media for any sign of Marcus, any new account, any hint that the surveillance was continuing. His manager had pulled him aside, concerned. Chukwu couldn't tell him the truth. He had told no one at work about Marcus, about the stalking, about any of it. The shame of it—the sense that he had somehow invited this through his own carelessness—kept him silent.

He was nineteen and exhausted in a way that sleep didn't fix. When he finally called his mother and told her everything, she insisted he see someone. What terrified Chukwu most was the possibility that Marcus was still out there, still watching, still waiting for the moment when Chukwu's guard dropped. And beneath that fear was something harder to name: the conviction that he deserved this, that his own actions had set it all in motion, and that no amount of caution would ever be enough to make him safe.
